newsitem.title: USA: TENNIS-MUSTER DOWNS PHILIPPOUSSIS TO REACH INDIAN WELLS SEMIS.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-MUSTER DOWNS PHILIPPOUSSIS TO REACH INDIAN WELLS SEMIS.

text.p: Clay court star Thomas Muster showed off his hardcourt prowess Friday in dismissing big-serving Australian Mark Philippoussis in the quarter-finals of the Champions Cup.
The second-seeded Austrian turned back the 32nd-ranked Philippoussis 6-3 7-6 (10-8) to take his place in the final four for his third semifinal in four tournaments this year.
"People say that he's obviously one of the best clay courters," Philippoussis said of the former French Open champion. "But, gee, looks like he plays pretty good on hardcourt as well."
The upset-ravaged top half of the draw lost its last remaining seeded player when 35th-ranked Jonas Bjorkman bounced 14th seed Alberto Berasategui of Spain 6-2 6-3 in another quarter-final.
In the semifinals, Bjorkman will meet either 43rd-ranked Czech Bohdan Ulihrach, who stunned top seed Pete Sampras Wednesday, or 50th-ranked Byron Black of Zimbabwe.

"It's wide open now for all three of us to make the final," Bjorkman, who won his first career title at Auckland in January, said in assessing his chances. "For the whole time in 1997, the guys from behind are getting a little bit closer to the top guys."
In the other quarter-final, third seed and defending champion Michael Chang takes on Frenchman Cedric Pioline for the right to face Muster.

Philippoussis was building momentum after winning the tournament in Scottsdale last week and upsetting Andre Agassi in the first round here. But Muster showed no fear of the Australian's monster serve and outplayed him with his rock solid game from the baseline.

"Philippoussis is what I expected, mostly big serves," said Muster. "I knew if I'm not going to miss too many groundstrokes, play a solid baseline game, I would be all right. Big servers mostly don't have a great baseline game."
In fact, it was Muster who was the steadier of the two from the service line, never giving Philippoussis a break opportunity in the 79-minute match.
Muster commited just seven unforced errors in the entire match and just one in a near perfect second set, while Philppoussis racked up 31 errors.
Despite the discrepancy in the error department, however, the latter stages of the tight second set had the large crowd fully into the match.
With Philippoussis at 5-6, 40-0, Muster fought back and reached his first match point when the Australian double faulted at deuce.

Muster thought he had the match won when Philippoussis smashed a lob that the second seed thought landed just beyond the baseline. But, in a move more common to clay play, Muster checked the mark and agreed with the call that Philippoussis had indeed hit a winning shot.
There were four more match points for Muster and one set point for Philippousis in the tiebreaker before the Austrian closed it out at 10-8.
